# Nile

> A functional TypeScript backend for small teams. Keep shipping as your backend grows with services, actions and a familiar place for every operation.

## Guide

- [Getting started](/nile/guide/start/getting-started.md): Build your first business operation with Nile.
- [Know where the next feature belongs](/nile/guide/start/application-structure.md): A small team should be able to open an unfamiliar feature and follow it. Use domains to give that work a home, services to list its public operations, and ordinary functions for the business rules behind them. This is a recommended organization, not a folder scanner. Nile executes the services and actions you explicitly register; it does not assign behavior to directory names.
- [Choose a runtime adapter](/nile/guide/start/runtime-adapters.md): Your services, actions, validation and Result handling stay the same across Nile's two HTTP adapters. Choose the adapter for the environment and HTTP integrations your application needs. Hono remains the default compatibility path. Updating Nile does not opt an existing application into Bun native. Native requires an explicit Bun runtime; a conflicting configuration fails at setup.
- [From routes to business operations](/nile/guide/start/from-rest.md): A growing product adds operations such as approving a submission, archiving a project or refunding a payment. Nile names those operations directly: projects.archive, submissions.approve, payments.refund. The goal is a consistent place for the team to work. You still design the operation, its input and its access policy. Nile gives it a common invocation shape rather than another per-operation route.
- [Migrate one domain at a time](/nile/guide/start/migration.md): Start with an operation your team understands. Keep its business logic and data layer, give it a Nile action boundary, and verify its existing behavior before moving more traffic.
- [Deploy the application you built](/nile/guide/start/deploy.md): Nile builds a request handler; your runtime starts and owns the listener. A long-running Bun or Node.js service is the straightforward deployment model.
- [Give each operation a clear boundary](/nile/guide/basics/actions.md): An action is a named business operation. Keep its description, input schema and handler together so a teammate can understand what it accepts and how it finishes without tracing a chain of route definitions. The example returns a project without persistence. In a real application, coordinate the business function or model from the handler and propagate its Result.
- [Group work by domain](/nile/guide/basics/services.md): A service gives related actions a recognizable home. Use domain names the team already uses: projects, tickets, billing or collaboration. As more operations arrive, people can start with the domain rather than search an unfamiliar route map. Pass services to createNileServer. Nile registers that list at startup and rejects duplicate service names or duplicate action names within a service. A service is an application grouping, not a separately deployed microservice. It does not create a database, process or network boundary. Your ordinary business functions and models can be shared through explicit imports or application resources.
- [Make ordinary failure paths easy to follow](/nile/guide/basics/errors-and-results.md): A team should be able to see how an operation can fail beside its business logic. Nile handlers return Ok(data) or Err(message) from slang-ts, so expected failures become explicit branches. The schema checks the input shape before the handler. The guard expresses an application rule. A real persistence call would live in the application's model or repository.
- [Share dependencies in a familiar place](/nile/guide/basics/context.md): A growing application often needs the same logger, database client or cache across many operations. Supply long-lived resources once and read them through Nile context instead of building a new dependency container for every action. Handlers receive context as their optional second argument: This fragment assumes a typed input and Ok imported from slang-ts. Logging happens where you configure or call it; a logger resource does not automatically create an audit record for every request.
- [Apply access rules consistently](/nile/guide/basics/auth.md): As more operations are added, a common policy boundary helps the team avoid repeating authentication code. Nile includes JWT verification; role, organization and resource-level authorization remain explicit application rules.
- [Reuse a policy across operations](/nile/guide/basics/hooks-and-pipelines.md): When several actions need the same check or transformation, put it in a recognizable pipeline step. That keeps the next operation small and makes the shared rule easier to review.
- [Call business operations from the frontend](/nile/guide/basics/client.md): The frontend can call projects.create by name while the backend keeps its service/action structure. The standalone client works wherever your application can use Fetch; it does not require React or a shared repository. baseUrl is the API prefix, not the /services endpoint. The client appends /services and sends the execution envelope.
- [Keep input contracts aligned](/nile/guide/basics/type-system.md): A growing team benefits when the action schema, TypeScript input and frontend call describe the same operation. Nile gives those pieces a common shape, with explicit boundaries.
- [Let tools inspect the operations you expose](/nile/guide/basics/discovery-and-agents.md): A predictable domain structure helps a coding agent find implementation files. Runtime discovery solves a different problem: an integration can inspect registered operations and their input descriptions before calling them. Nile provides explore and schema intents. It does not include an MCP server, an autonomous agent runtime or automatic tool registration. Your integration decides which operations a tool can call and carries the caller's credentials.
- [Invoke an operation](/nile/guide/basics/interacting.md): All action calls use POST {baseUrl}/services. With rest.baseUrl: "/api", send: Execution requires a specific service and action; wildcards are for discovery. Nile checks the envelope, runs the action pipeline and maps its Result to the HTTP response. An action failure has status: false, its error message and data: {}. Engine failures, including a missing action, normally return HTTP 400. Invalid request envelopes also return 400; a missing HTTP route returns 404. Check the envelope as well as the HTTP response. See errors and Results.
- [Receive files through an action](/nile/guide/basics/uploads.md): Multipart uploads use the same POST /api/services endpoint as JSON operations. Nile parses fields and files and applies configured file limits; the action decides what the upload means and where it is stored.
- [Serve public assets when needed](/nile/guide/basics/file-serving.md): For a small application, Nile can expose a local public asset directory without another HTTP service. Both adapters support the same configuration: The default directory is ./assets, relative to the application's working directory. A file at assets/logo.png is available at GET /assets/logo.png; the asset namespace is independent of rest.baseUrl. Bun native uses Bun file responses and supports GET/HEAD. Hono selects its runtime-specific static adapter. Select runtime: "bun" or runtime: "node" explicitly; native: true requires Bun.
- [Keep HTTP-specific work in a route](/nile/guide/basics/custom-routes.md): Use actions for business operations, and ordinary HTTP routes when an integration expects a particular URL, method or response. Webhooks, authentication callbacks and streaming endpoints can live beside Nile's action API.
- [Server setup](/nile/guide/internals/server.md): createNileServer registers your application, creates context and prepares the selected HTTP adapter. It does not start a network listener. This keeps application setup separate from deployment.
- [Data access](/nile/guide/internals/db/index.md): Keep business operations easy to follow: an action handles its input and application policy, an ordinary domain function implements the rule, and a model/repository owns data access. This is a useful convention, not a runtime restriction. Nile does not require a particular ORM or database. The application structure guide shows how these modules fit together as the operation count grows.
- [createModel](/nile/guide/internals/db/create-model.md): Use createModel when a Drizzle-backed domain needs familiar CRUD operations. Keep custom business queries in ordinary model functions rather than forcing every operation through a generic helper.
- [Logging](/nile/guide/internals/logging.md): A consistent log format helps a small team follow a failure back to the operation that produced it. Nile includes a structured logger; supply it through resources so actions, hooks and error helpers can use the same convention.
- [Execution engine](/nile/guide/internals/engine.md): The engine gives every business operation the same execution path. A team can review input checks, reusable policy and the handler without learning a different convention for each service.
- [HTTP transport](/nile/guide/internals/rest.md): Nile exposes registered business operations through POST {baseUrl}/services. The transport parses input, applies configured HTTP policies and sends an operation to the engine. The same action organization works with Bun native and the Hono adapter.
- [CORS](/nile/guide/internals/cors.md): CORS controls which browser origins may read responses. Configure it once for the application, then override it only where an operation needs a different policy. It does not prevent non-browser callers from invoking an action and must not replace authorization.
- [FAQ](/nile/guide/reference/faq.md)
- [Operating a Nile application](/nile/guide/reference/operations.md): Nile keeps business operations in services and actions. HTTP, direct calls and WebSockets use the same engine. Schedules and function controls support background work without requiring a second application architecture.
- [Actions and messages over Socket.IO](/nile/guide/reference/realtime.md): Nile keeps transport configuration under rest, rpc and websocket. REST and sockets can run together; action invocations use the same validation, hooks, authentication and execution pipeline. Socket.IO provides connection handling beneath the Nile API.
- [A measured shopping workflow](/nile/guide/reference/performance.md): A growing backend needs to do more than return hello world. This comparison runs an authenticated ecommerce workflow across 300 business operations: 50 shops with catalog, product, cart, quote, checkout and order operations. The results below describe one recorded workload on an actively used PC. They are not maximum-throughput measurements or a universal ranking of frameworks. Choose an application structure your team can maintain, and measure your own workload before making capacity decisions. !<a href="/nile/benchmarks/benchmark-validated.svg">Six-round ecommerce throughput averages with shared Zod payload validation enabled.</a>
- [Choosing Nile](/nile/guide/reference/framework-comparison.md): Choose Nile when a small team wants a consistent place for growing business operations, while keeping its business logic in ordinary TypeScript functions. A service groups related actions. Each action names an operation, can validate its input and returns an explicit Result. Shared context and hooks let the team apply dependencies and policies consistently. Learn one operation’s shape, then follow the same path through the next domain.
- [Documentation for coding agents](/nile/guide/reference/llms-txt.md): Nile's <a href="/nile/llms.txt">llms.txt</a> lists the public guides, and <a href="/nile/llms-full.txt">llms-full.txt</a> contains the documentation bundle. Use them to give a coding assistant the current service/action conventions, runtime APIs and examples before it changes an application. The npm package also includes SKILL.md and these generated documentation files under docs/. Follow the application's own instructions and check its existing service registry before adding another operation. Nile is listed on Context7. If your assistant has Context7 configured, it can retrieve library documentation through that integration. Availability and retrieved versions depend on that service and your assistant setup. Documentation access is separate from runtime API discovery. Reading these files does not give an agent credentials or permission to execute an application's actions.
- [LLMs Full](/nile/guide/reference/llms-full-txt.md): <a href="/nile/llms-full.txt">Read the full documentation bundle</a>
